articles.title: Angel Reese’s WNBA Finals showed how criticism of her play becomes an accusation of racism
articles.summary: Angel Reese earned praise for her best Finals games, but her late-series struggles exposed the limits of a fan defense built around dismissing critics as haters.
articles.body: People often accuse me of "hating on" Angel Reese. I reject that label because it misrepresents both who I am and what I do. After spending more than two weeks flying back and forth between San Francisco and Atlanta to cover the 2026 WNBA Finals, I came away more convinced of something I’ve noticed throughout my coverage of Reese: For many of her defenders, criticizing her quickly becomes a referendum on the person doing the criticizing.\ WHY ISN'T ANGEL REESE HELD TO CAITLIN CLARK'S STANDARD WHEN FANS ATTACK HER TEAMMATES? During the Finals, I repeatedly encountered the same accusation on social media: My criticism of Reese meant I had a problem with Black women. I received hundreds of posts saying that I am a racist for daring to criticize Reese. One post in particular caught my attention. On Oct. 17, an account called Apex Jones posted a five-minute, 39-second video promising to "EXPOSE Outkick and Dan Zaksheske for targeting Angel Reese for YEARS." The accompanying post declared, "Outkick is anti-WNBA and anti-Black Women." The account has nearly 10,000 followers on X, and the post drew about 1,100 likes and more than 220 reposts. The video included questions I asked Reese about her move from Chicago to Atlanta. "What role did you play in that trade?" I asked on Oct. 16, media day for the WNBA Finals. Reese said Chicago was trading her and worked with her on the destination. Atlanta wanted her, and she wanted Atlanta. I followed up by asking how she balanced staying somewhere to build a winner with seeking an opportunity to win elsewhere. She discussed her move from Maryland to LSU and wanting a coach who would push her. I did my job: I asked her questions and she gave answers. But Apex Jones argued that my coverage was going to make Reese look bad either way. When Chicago traded her, I questioned her value. When she reached the Finals with Atlanta, I questioned what joining an established winner said about her winning mentality. His accusation was that I changed the argument while keeping the same negative conclusion. His criticism leaves out half of what I wrote. In April, I argued that either Chicago didn’t value Reese the way her biggest cheerleaders did, or she had pushed for a trade. "It’s possible that Reese demanded a trade from Chicago," I wrote at the time. Asking her in October what role she played in the move followed directly from the question I had raised six months earlier. ANGEL REESE’S LATEST WNBA CONTROVERSY SHOWS HOW VICTIMHOOD BECAME CENTRAL TO HER BRAND I also gave Reese an opportunity to address a criticism many people had raised: that she had forced her way out of Chicago to chase a ring with Atlanta. I included her explanation in my coverage. Giving her the chance to answer her critics is part of covering her fairly. People are free to disagree with my assessment of Reese or the questions I ask her. But the claim that I have a problem with Black women requires more than disagreement with my coverage of one basketball player. She is an individual, and holding her accountable for what she says and does isn’t an attack on Black women. Have I been hard on Angel Reese? Absolutely. My columns contain pointed opinions, and I use sarcasm in my social posts. But disagreement with the tone doesn't answer the underlying questions. Angel Reese has earned the attention Love her or hate her, Reese draws strong reactions from people. That is a valuable skill in professional sports, especially in 2026. She deserves credit for that. Another criticism I've heard many times is that I'm "obsessed" with Angel Reese. The truth is that the audience is obsessed with Reese. My post about Reese arriving for Game 5 wearing a "Protect Black Women" shirt generated more than 1.7 million impressions and 3,400 replies on X. Another criticizing a play in Game 2 drew nearly a million impressions and more than 1,300 replies. People were watching, arguing and responding. If posts and stories about her didn't draw significant interest, I wouldn’t cover her nearly as much. Now, as far as how I cover Reese, that depends on what she says and does. If she talks trash and then struggles, I'm going to call her out. If she plays a great game, I'll say that, too. After Game 2, the headline of my story was, "Angel Reese dominates Game 2 as Atlanta Dream even WNBA Finals against Golden State Valkyries." After Game 3, my headline read: "Angel Reese delivers another double-double as Atlanta Dream take 2–1 lead in WNBA Finals." Reese played incredibly well in Games 2 and 3 and helped carry Atlanta to those two victories. I had no problem saying it, either. And I've written about Reese's strong performances in the past. In June 2025, after a strong stretch in Chicago, I wrote: "I feel a duty to point it out when Reese does well" in a story headlined, "Angel Reese Posts Another Strong Performance, Will It Quiet The Haters?" Interestingly, these stories never seem to come up when people are labeling me as a racist. Reese's antics and play drove the narrative As much as people like to call out my reporting and writing as setting the narrative, the truth is that Reese determines the narrative. After Game 3, Reese taunted Golden State with a "too small" gesture, followed by sarcastically waving at them as they left the court. Ahead of Game 4, she said she could "take their confidence and just try to do whatever to mess them up." I attended the postgame press conferences featuring Reese after nearly every Finals game. After Games 2 and 3, she sounded like a player who had already won a championship. That's fine. Talk your talk. But if you want the smoke, you better back it up. Reese didn't. Over the final four games of the WNBA Finals, Reese scored 38 points on 12-for-45 shooting. She shot 26.7 percent from the field and committed 19 turnovers. She had more turnovers than made field goals in each of those four games. Thus, my tone changed. "Angel Reese struggles badly after bold comments as Valkyries beat Dream to even WNBA Finals," my headline read after Game 4. Was that me inventing a narrative? No. Reese taunted her opponents, explained how she was in their heads, and then proceeded to score 8 points on 2-for-12 shooting. But, apparently, pointing that out is racist? In Game 7, Valkyries star Gabby Williams scored 28 points in the second half. Reese scored 3 in the second half, making just one field goal. Reese said during the Finals that players become great when they "win and impact winning." She simply didn't do that when her team needed her most. If she wants to be a superstar and treated like one of the best players in the WNBA, she can't disappear when a championship is on the line. For some fans, though, the argument seems to end at identifying a critic as a hater. That saves them the trouble of explaining her poor performance. Accountability has to leave room for credit There is something else I have learned covering Reese: Her teammates and coaches ride for her. I was in Albany after LSU lost to Iowa in the 2024 Elite Eight. Flau'jae Johnson and Hailey Van Lith strongly defended Reese. "Y’all do not get to Angel Reese. So you might want to throw the towel in because you’re wasting your energy," Van Lith said. She also praised Reese’s toughness and described her continuing to show up despite the hostility. Johnson said Reese is a "caring, loving person." Her coaches have shown that support, too. Kim Mulkey, who coached Reese at LSU, was in Atlanta cheering her on during Game 3 of the Finals. In May, Dream head coach Karl Smesko said, "She wants to be held accountable. I mean, she’s an All-Star player, but she wants to be the best player." Additionally, Reese deserves credit for making herself available to the media after every Finals game. Toward the end of games, reporters received emails listing the players scheduled for the postgame podium, usually that night’s top performers. More than once, Reese wasn’t listed, but she appeared anyway. As Atlanta’s most prominent player, she should have been there regardless of performance. Still, I was surprised the Dream made her available every time, especially when she wasn't on the initial list. That was perhaps the most impressive thing I noticed about both Reese and the Dream during the WNBA Finals. After Game 4, Reese took responsibility for her poor performance and said, "I’ll just be better." That's what I want to hear more often from Reese. Unfortunately, after Game 5, she changed her tune. Asked about her eight shot attempts and Golden State’s defense, Reese pointed to the officiating. "A lot of us are getting fouled, and they are not calling it," Reese said. She acknowledged Atlanta’s shooting struggles elsewhere in the press conference, but complaining about referees after a second straight bad game isn't the best look. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! My own experience covering Reese also raises questions about how she handles criticism. During the Finals, I noticed she had blocked me on X. I’m a reporter covering the WNBA. I have never tweeted at her or tagged her in a post. Yes, I post about Reese because that's part of my job. And I understand blocking internet trolls who direct offensive language at you. But there is a massive distinction between online trolls and a reporter criticizing your performances and public statements without ever contacting you on the platform. To me, blocking that reporter suggests a willingness to shut out coverage she doesn’t like. The spotlight comes with scrutiny Here's my advice to Angel Reese: If you want to be treated like a superstar, accept being evaluated like one. When you taunt opponents and then struggle, both belong in the story. Own the performances that fall short as readily as you celebrate the ones that live up to your expectations. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD And here’s my advice to Angel Reese fans: Root for her to succeed. And go ahead and defend her when you think criticism is unfair. But explain why it’s unfair. Calling me a hater or a racist isn’t a substitute for a counterargument. If you believe Reese is one of the best players in the WNBA, hold her to that standard, too. You can support her without defending everything she says and does. And please, for the love of God, stop claiming that criticism of Angel Reese amounts to criticism of all Black women.

articles.title: Latest 2027 Men's NCAA Tournament Bracket Projections
articles.summary: Many will say that updating projections for the men's NCAA tournament a mere week into the 2026-27 regular season is nothing short of lunacy.
articles.body:
Many will say that updating projections for the men's NCAA tournament a mere week into the 2026-27 regular season is nothing short of lunacy.

We would counter that those people don't know how to have fun.

Because, yes, that's all bracketology is for at least the first month of the regular season: Fun.

We won't have NET rankings for another few weeks—last year's initial rankings were released on Dec. 1—which means "quads" won't be part of the discourse just yet. Even when those rankings arrive, there's little reason to expect them to resemble the final version some 100 days later.

For the diehards, though, bracketology is all about the season-long journey—the constant twists and turns that eventually bring us to the final product. And that journey began eight days ago.

Remember, results from the first half of November mean just as much to the selection committee as the results from the first half of March. In fact, one could easily argue these early results are even more important , because they establish the baseline for how teams will be judged for the rest of the season.

So, let's have some fun while recapping and (over)reacting to some of the biggest developments from the first week back on the hardwood.

Later in the season, automatic bids will be determined by conference record. For now, they are determined by KenPom ranking.

Also, please forgive any first-round pairings which are rematches of scheduled nonconference games. We won't start worrying about avoiding those until shortly after Feast Week.

If you don't love the ordering of these top seven teams, rest assured there will be plenty of head-to-head showdowns within this tier to help us sort everything out.

Between now and Dec. 1, Duke will face Michigan State in the Champions Classic on Nov. 10, host Illinois on Nov. 17, take on Connecticut in Las Vegas on Nov. 25 and travel to Florida for the headliner of the ACC-SEC Challenge on Dec. 1.

Throw in UConn facing Illinois in Chicago on Dec. 4 before hosting Kansas on Dec. 12, conference clashes between Illinois and Michigan State and between Houston and Kansas in early February, and the possibility of Florida facing Houston and Kansas on consecutive days in the Players Era 8, and you have a potential 10 games between No. 1 seed contenders.

In particular, circle Duke-Illinois and Duke-Florida on your calendar. Those matchups feature our top three teams in the country, and both will be played on campus—making them all the more fun to watch.

10 Words on Each of the 10 'Bubbliest' Teams

Fifth-to-Last In : Utah State Aggies—Head coach keeps changing, but this offense remains super efficient.

Fourth-to-Last In : VCU Rams—Heartbreaking loss at Memphis, but the Rams looked the part.

Third-to-Last In : Oklahoma State Cowboys—That 50-point shellacking of Queens was quite the early statement.

Second-to-Last In : Xavier Musketeers—Unremarkable competition, but this defense appears to be much improved.

Last Team In : Notre Dame Fighting Irish—Got to get 'em in after beating Villanova in Rome.

First Team Out : Virginia Tech Hokies—Blew out Coppin State and Mercer; faces Iowa on Tuesday.

Second Team Out : Boise State Broncos—Dropped a hundo on Butler; big opportunity against Nebraska ahead.

Third Team Out : Nevada Wolf Pack—Overtime win over Saint Mary's could be one to remember.

Fourth Team Out : Florida State Seminoles—Freshman big man Marcis Ponder could help end tourney drought.

Fifth Team Out : Providence Friars—Couldn't buy a bucket in the neutral loss to Nebraska.

7 Teams in the Projected Field : 1. Duke, 8. Virginia, 12. Louisville, 23. Miami (FL), 33. North Carolina, 48. Clemson, 53. Notre Dame

Also Considered : Virginia Tech, Florida State

For the most part, the ACC spent the opening week beating up on nobodies in buy games.

At any rate, through the end of play on Saturday, the league was 34-2 overall, but 1-2 against teams in the KenPom top 150.

The losses were Miami falling by 10 to No. 1-ranked Florida and Wake Forest getting smoked at No. 24 Vanderbilt, both of which were the expected outcomes.

Notre Dame beating Villanova in Rome, though?

That's arguably the Fighting Irish's most impressive win since hiring Micah Shrewsberry as their head coach shortly after the 2022-23 campaign ended.

If name confusion is commonplace in your life, best of luck with Notre Dame's big three of Braeden Smith, Braeden Shrewsberry and Brady Koehler. Each member of that trio went for at least 15 points against Villanova. And in their first game of the season on US soil, Shrewsberry and Koehler each scored 17 while Smith tallied 10 assists in a rout of Mercyhurst.

Give it a few more days and we'll find out in a big way just how legitimate this team is. They face Florida in the opening round of the Players Era 8 on Nov. 17, could draw Houston the following day and might even run into Kansas on the 19th.

Most likely, they'll lose to Florida, beat Rutgers on Wednesday and run into West Virginia or Auburn in the fifth-place game. But what a three-day stretch that could be for the Irish.

Elsewhere, goodness gracious did Virginia ever put a thumping on Arkansas on Sunday afternoon. We had the Cavaliers as a No. 4 seed in the preseason, but they have to vault to the back of the No. 2 seed line for that statement victory.

10 Teams in the Projected Field : 5. Houston, 7. Kansas, 10. Arizona, 19. Texas Tech, 20. BYU, 21. Iowa State, 25. Baylor, 41. West Virginia, 44. TCU, 51. Oklahoma State

Also Considered : UCF, Cincinnati, Arizona State

Biggest Development : Iowa State upended by Memphis

It was a rocky first 48 hours for the Big 12.

Despite 38 points from Ivan Kharchenkov, preseason No. 1 seed Arizona lost an old Pac-12 rivalry game with UCLA. Kansas State cemented itself as the likely worst team in the conference with an immediate home loss to South Dakota State. And though UCF (vs. Florida Gulf Coast) and Utah (vs. Long Beach State) ultimately prevailed, they both threatened to suffer what would have been brutal losses.

BYU did score a statement win over Ohio State behind 35 points from Rob Wright III. But perhaps the most impactful result was Iowa State (preseason KenPom No. 6) losing to Memphis (preseason KenPom No. 86) in Sioux Falls, South Dakota.

It was a tight one throughout, played entirely within a 12-point window and tied at 69-69 with a little over three minutes to go. That's when Tigers lead guard Jayden Reid took over, single-handedly outscoring the Cyclones 11-7 down the stretch on his way to 26 points.

One major asterisk is that Iowa State didn't have Killyan Toure, but that's going to be the case for the first half of the season as he works his way back from shoulder surgery.

The Cyclones did have Tamin Lipsey available, though, after his summer with the Indiana Pacers. But even that fifth-year point guard was no answer for Reid.

Iowa State was a No. 3 seed in our preseason projection, but they take an early tumble to the No. 6 seed line. We shall see if they can bounce back with a strong run through the Players Era 16 during Feast Week.

6 Teams in the Projected Field : 4. Connecticut, 16. St. John's, 28. Marquette, 39. Villanova, 47. Creighton, 52. Xavier

Also Considered : Providence, Georgetown, DePaul

Biggest Development : UConn returns to the No. 1 seed line

The final score (85-77) doesn't scream "beat down," but Connecticut put a hurtin' on reigning national champion Michigan on Friday night in Boston.

Top returnees Braylon Mullins and Silas Demary Jr. went for 23 and 21 points, respectively, while freshman phenom Colben Landrew pitched in 14 points and eight rebounds. That backcourt trio is going to be one of the best in the country.

And it sounds like the trio might be a quartet sooner than expected? CBS Sports' Matt Norlander casually mentioned after the win that Solo Ball (wrist) looked good in warmups and could be back in action "in the next month or so." Considering we entered the season unsure if Ball would be able to play at all, that's quite the early development.

Regardless of whether Ball does return before the start of Big East play, the Huskies have a preposterously difficult row to hoe, facing Ohio State (Nov. 13), Arizona (Nov. 18), Duke (Nov. 25), Illinois (Dec. 4), Kansas (Dec. 12) and Virginia (Dec. 20) between now and Christmas.

It's the toughest nonconference schedule in the country, but they've started it out with a bang.

Someone had to replace Arizona on the No. 1 seed line, and it is now Connecticut's spot to lose.

11 Teams in the Projected Field : 3. Illinois, 6. Michigan State, 15. UCLA, 18. Nebraska, 26. Michigan, 31. USC, 32. Indiana, 34. Ohio State, 35. Iowa, 37. Minnesota, 38. Wisconsin

Biggest Development : Purdue's Tournament Streak in Early Jeopardy

Though a far cry from Kansas, Michigan State and Gonzaga with at least 27 consecutive NCAA tournament appearances apiece, Purdue has the fourth-longest active dancing streak, partaking in each of the last 11 tournaments.

Can the Boilermakers bounce back from a disastrous start to this season, though?

The opener against Gonzaga in Las Vegas was always likely to result in a loss, considering the Zags were ranked No. 15 in the preseason poll while Purdue is adjusting to life after Braden Smith, Fletcher Loyer and Trey Kaufman-Renn. And though it was a competitive game, Purdue did start out 0-1 for the first time since 2012-13.

What definitely was not supposed to be a loss, however, was the subsequent home game against Valparaiso. But after the Beacons hit buzzer-beating three-pointers to both extend the game at the end of the first overtime and win the game at the end of the second overtime, Purdue fell to 0-2 for the first time since 1976-77.

On the plus side, that squad 50 years ago recovered to finish 19–9 and reach a 32-team NCAA tournament. Maybe this year's bunch can turn things around to secure one of the 76 spots up for grabs.

But Purdue is in previously uncharted waters under Matt Painter.

13 Teams in the Projected Field : 2. Florida, 11. Texas, 13. Alabama, 14. Tennessee, 17. Vanderbilt, 22. Kentucky, 24. Auburn, 27. Texas A&M, 30. Arkansas, 36. Georgia, 42. LSU, 43. Ole Miss, 45. Missouri

Biggest Development : Oklahoma Lost to Whom?!

For the most part, things are proceeding as expected for the SEC.

The league entered the season projected for 13 bids, and that still appears to be the case. They've already made some strong early impressions at the expense of the ACC, with Florida beating Miami and Vanderbilt trouncing Wake Forest—though Virginia leveled the scales a bit with its pulverization of Arkansas.

But amid what has otherwise been a strong start, Oklahoma already suffered what might be the worst loss of the entire season.

Hosting preseason KenPom No. 299 East Texas A&M, the Sooners were projected to win 90-62, given a 99 percent chance of victory. Instead, they completely no-showed on offense for a 68-64 loss.

At least a few times per month, we'll see a team lose when KenPom has its victory probability in the 90-97 percent range.

Even Virginia was only at 97 percent for its loss to UMBC in 2018, while Purdue was at 98 percent when it lost to Fairleigh Dickinson in 2023.

I clicked day-by-day through the past three seasons on KenPom and only found one other case of a team losing in spite of a win probability of at least 99 percent. Coincidentally, it was also a disastrous SEC result, when Mississippi State lost to Southern on Dec. 3, 2023 .

Notably, that flub didn't end the Bulldogs' season. They still made the Dance as a No. 8 seed, thanks to a few marquee wins in league play. Perhaps Oklahoma, too, can recover from this early embarrassment.

However, after entering the year as a No. 9 seed, the Sooners will have to play their way back into the conversation with a strong run through the rest of what isn't a great nonconference schedule.

Mid-Majors Summary (A10, AAC, MVC, MWC, P12, WCC)

8 Teams in the Projected Field : 9. Gonzaga, 29. Saint Louis, 40. Memphis, 46. Grand Canyon, 49. Utah State, 50. VCU, 54. Saint Mary's, 57. Murray State

Also Considered : Boise State, Nevada, New Mexico, San Diego State

Biggest Development : Memphis Is a Problem Again

Memphis had a brutal season last year, going 13-19 overall. It was the Tigers' first losing record since going 15-16 in 1999-2000 and their worst winning percentage since going 6-20 in 1969-70.

But after months of Penny Hardaway sitting prominently on any "hot seat rankings" type of list, Memphis stuck with him for at least one more year, and the early returns have been fantastic.

In the Big 12 section, we discussed the Tigers' win over Iowa State, in which Northwestern transfer Jayden Reid led the way with 26 points.

He was even bigger in the 89-88 victory over VCU on Saturday, though. Reid finished with 32 points, seven assists and three steals. He hit a massive game-tying three-pointer with a little over a minute remaining and followed it up with the game-tying and game-winning free throws with 5.7 seconds left on the clock.

He scored their final 11 points against the Cyclones and had 12 of their final 17 points against the Rams.

That's two big wins, but their journey has only just begun.

Memphis plays at Vanderbilt on Tuesday and hosts Louisville on Sunday for two more massive opportunities before our next projection. The Tigers will also play road games at Baylor and Texas, face Grand Canyon and Utah State, and play neutral-site games against Dayton, Penn State and either Wake Forest or Mississippi State.

That's nothing new, of course. They've been scheduling aggressively for six years now, and faring well against that gauntlet two seasons ago is what got them a No. 5 seed in the Dance. They might be gearing up to do it again.

21 Teams in the Projected Field : 55. High Point, 56. UC San Diego, 58. Akron, 59. McNeese, 60. UNC Wilmington, 61. Wright State, 62. Western Kentucky, 63. Furman, 64. Montana State, 65. Yale, 66. Central Arkansas, 67. Old Dominion, 68. Vermont, 69. Howard, 70. Queens, 71. South Dakota State, 72. American, 73. Bethune-Cookman, 74. Iona, 75. Tennessee State, 76. Long Island

Biggest Development : Wright State's Hottest Start Ever?

The Wright State Raiders won their season opener against Air Force in blowout fashion, 102-71. Dominic Pangonis almost could not miss en route to his 30 points, needing just 10 field-goal attempts and seven free-throw attempts to get there.

They followed it up with a similarly sized 97-71 beatdown of Florida Atlantic on Friday. The starting five shot a combined 24-for-30 (80.0 percent) from inside the arc in a game that was over in a hurry.

Neither result was much of a needle-mover. The home win over AFA will certainly be a Quad 4 result when NET rankings come out. The home win over FAU figures to land somewhere near the border between Quad 3 and Quad 4.

But after two games against D-I competition, Wright State is 2-0 with a plus-57 point differential—which is the furthest thing from par for the course.

In their previous 39 seasons as a D-I program, they started out 0-2 against D-I foes twice as many times (14) as they started 2-0 (seven). And prior to this, Wright State never had a point differential north of 30 through two games.

Could this be a breakthrough year for a team that, as a No. 14 seed, gave Virginia a run for its money in the first round of the 2026 NCAA tournament?

The Raiders certainly look like the cream of the Horizon League crop thus far.

articles.title: 5 Rising Stars Who Could Make Their First All-NBA Team
articles.summary: It's really hard to make an All-NBA team, a fact made plain when you consider the quality of this season's potential first-timers.
articles.body:
It's really hard to make an All-NBA team, a fact made plain when you consider the quality of this season's potential first-timers.

Cooper Flagg is the most promising prospect this side of Victor Wembanyama, Alperen Sengun is leading one of the early season's top threats and Scottie Barnes is easily one of the best two-way stars in the league. For various reasons, none of them has ever managed to earn an All-NBA nod.

Clearing that bar requires statistical excellence, some amount of team success and, sometimes, a little patience. Voters tend to reward the old guard before they recognize fresher faces.

Though we're still in the early part of the 2026-27 season, several ascending newbies are making their cases undeniable. The 65-game rule has already knocked out some of the usual suspects, opening the door wider for a flood of first-time honorees.

If Cooper Flagg maintains this pace, he could join LeBron James, Kobe Bryant, Luka Dončić and Carl Braun as players to earn All-NBA honors in their age-20 seasons.

It's just like everyone said during Flagg's breakout rookie season last year: This kid could be the next Carl Braun.

Flagg's offense has leveled up in his second year, helped partially by the presence of Kyrie Irving's playmaking but mostly by organic growth. His pull-up mid-ranger is automatic now, he's getting to the foul line at will and Flagg is seeing the floor even better as a facilitator, averaging about 2.0 more assists per game than he did a year ago.

With his highly touted defensive disruption showing through more clearly and the Dallas Mavericks exceeding expectations by playing winning basketball, Flagg's numbers—23.9 points, 6.8 rebounds, 6.4 assists, 2.3 steals and 0.9 blocks—cannot be dismissed as empty.

Perhaps more importantly, they're already better than any produced during Carl Braun's 13-year career.

Scottie Barnes has a pair of All-Star trips and earned an All-Defensive nod last season, so he's no stranger to individual awards. The main one he's missing, an All-NBA honor, feels inevitable.

The 25-year-old is putting up 23.5 points, 7.6 rebounds, 5.1 assists and 2.3 steals per game in his sixth season, carrying over the two-way dominance he displayed during last year's relatively brief playoff run.

Long a disruptive defensive force who piles up stocks, the rangy forward is making his biggest strides on the offensive end. It'll be a shock if he doesn't maintain a scoring average north of 20.0 points per game—even after Kawhi Leonard returns from injury.

Though Barnes continues to struggle as a three-point shooter, he's on track to average a career-high 6.8 free-throw attempts per 36 minutes. Those extra trips to the line should help offset his iffy long-range shooting and maintain solid scoring efficiency.

The last factor is durability, which takes on real importance with the league's minimum-games threshold. Barnes logged 80 appearances last year and has played at least 65 games in every season of his career but one.

Knock on wood, but health seems less likely to derail his All-NBA chances than those of most other players.

If the season ended today, Alperen Sengun would have the league's eighth-highest Value Over Replacement Player figure. That should be more than good enough to get the two-time All-Star into the All-NBA club.

There are still another 70-something games to go, so no hardware will be awarded any time soon. But Sengun's strong start is fueling a stellar Houston Rockets team that could very easily finish atop the Western Conference. That team-related achievement should combine with career-best numbers to get the job done.

So far, Sengun is putting up his typical 20-ish points per game and flirting with double-doubles on most nights. While that's not new, his improved facilitation and perimeter accuracy are. On pace to blow away his previous career bests with 50.0 percent shooting from long range (we know that's coming down) and 7.8 assists per game, the sixth-year big man is playing at a personal peak.

Just 24 and still adding layers to an already All-Star-worthy game, Sengun (who, like Barnes, has only fallen below the 65-game mark once in five previous years) feels like a lock.

Coming into the season, Avdija's potential role on a revamped Portland Trail Blazers team was a concern. After emerging as a star-level offensive fulcrum in 2025-26, the hard-charging forward figured to lose on-ball reps to new addition Ja Morant and returning franchise icon Damian Lillard.

An injury knocked out the former while a tweaked role moved the latter off the ball a bit more, but the real reason the 25-year-old profiles as an All-NBA first-timer is the Blazers' recognition that it would be wildly irresponsible to sideline their best player.

Avdija led the league in drives per game last year and ranks a solid second this time around. Nobody averages more assists per game on drives or gets to the foul line when attacking downhill more often. Though his usage and field-goal attempt rates are down by a fraction, his per-game averages of 22.3 points and 6.3 assists are virtually unchanged from a year ago.

As an added bonus, he is turning the ball over less frequently than he has since developing into a first option and has cultivated excellent two-man chemistry with Lillard.

The most important figure on a surprisingly good Blazers squad, Avdija is well on his way to finishing the season on an All-NBA team.

Teammate Luka Dončić is getting all the (deserved) press for his historic start, but Austin Reaves hasn't exactly faded into the background as the Los Angeles Lakers' second elite offensive option.

Dončić has missed two games so far this year, and while Reaves' efforts in the first, an easy 16-point win over the Clippers, didn't impress, he used the second to reaffirm his status as a dominant driver of offense.

On Nov. 8, Reaves racked up 43 points without Dončić, carrying the Lakers to an impressive five-point victory over the Detroit Pistons and their top-five defense. That effort contributed to what is so far a career-best 25.3 points per game scoring average.

A spectacular 50.8/41.3/90.9 shooting split has the 28-year-old on track to post a true shooting percentage of at least 60.0 percent for the sixth straight year.

While Reaves will only be the Lakers' No. 1 threat on nights Dončić is out of action, he's shown enough over the last couple of seasons to prove he's capable of stepping into that role whenever required. If he can stay healthy, he'll mix those kinds of nights with a ton of efficient second-option games to break through as an All-NBA first-timer.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: Laugh at Jon Scheyer's March failures while you can ... Duke's breakthrough is coming
articles.summary: With another loaded roster and a national championship in his sights, it's only a matter of time before Scheyer silences his critics.
articles.body:
Here's some hard truth for Duke haters who take delight in portraying Jon Scheyer as a March choke artist: He's going to shed that label someday.

Maybe not this year. Maybe not even next year. But rest assured, Scheyer's crowning moment is coming. An elite coach who keeps assembling star-laden rosters and molding those teams into powerhouses is eventually going to break through.

After back-to-back seasons of winning 35 games and sweeping the ACC regular season and tournament titles, Duke is poised to pick up where it left off. A Blue Devils team featuring a mix of heralded freshmen and March-tested veterans enters Tuesday night's Champions Classic matchup against Michigan State as the No. 2 team in the AP Top 25 and oddsmakers' co-favorite to win the national title.

Scheyer, 38, won't have another chance to silence his critics until the brackets are unveiled this March, but the Michigan State game is a significant early barometer for his Blue Devils. A neutral-court win over the fifth-ranked Spartans would validate Duke's preseason hype and solidify the Blue Devils as a leading title contender.

The best possible outcome for Scheyer might be Duke having to protect a narrow lead against a quality opponent on a big stage. That's exactly the scenario that has exposed Duke's shoddy decision making and issues executing late-game offense in March the past few years.

Scheyer has mostly made the impossible task of replacing a coaching icon look easy throughout his four-plus seasons as Duke's head coach, but there's no denying that Mike Krzyzewski's handpicked successor has underwhelmed on the NCAA tournament stage. Cooper Flagg, Cameron Boozer, Kon Knueppel and eight other NBA draft picks have all passed through Durham during Scheyer's tenure without experiencing the thrill of playing on the first Monday night in April.

Three years ago, a 27-win Duke team needed only to fend off 11th-seeded NC State to advance to Scheyer's first Final Four. The heavily favored Blue Devils shot miserably and surrendered 55 second-half points to turn a gift-wrapped opportunity into an Elite Eight gut punch.

Two years ago, the Flagg-Knueppel Blue Devils faced Houston in the Final Four and famously led by 14 with 8:17 left and by six with less than a minute to go. Duke then unraveled when facing game pressure for one of the few times all season and Flagg misfired on a short pull-up jumper when given a final chance to preserve his team's title hopes.

Last March, Duke built a 19-point lead late in the Elite Eight against UConn and still led by two with possession of the ball and 10 seconds to go. A Cayden Boozer turnover led to a highlight that will be replayed for decades — a 35-footer from UConn's Braylon Mullins that sent the Huskies to the Final Four and ended another promising Duke season in heartbreak.

The blowback after the UConn collapse was immediate and overwhelming. Observers who sought a common denominator among Duke's NCAA tournament meltdowns found only one.

"Duke officially has a Jon Scheyer March problem," SiriusXM host Adam Schein told his audience .

"Of course, he's to blame," podcast host Mark Titus said . "He sits there and watches it happen, watches it unfold."

In the most scorching take of all, college sports reporter Matt Fortuna posted to X , "Jon Scheyer has underachieved more at Duke than Hubert Davis did at North Carolina."

To compare the tenures of Scheyer and Davis, of course, is laughable. Scheyer has a 126-25 record as Duke head coach and amassed five ACC regular-season or tournament titles in his first four seasons. Davis spearheaded the Tar Heels' surprise run to the title game in his debut season, but three of his five seasons as North Carolina head coach ended with his team either missing the NCAA tournament or failing to advance beyond the round of 64.

It's also important to remember how many elite coaches faced a similar narrative to the one now foisted upon Scheyer.

Jay Wright was known as an NCAA tournament underachiever until Villanova steamrolled its way to national championships in 2016 and 2018.

Bill Self once faced similar criticism before Kansas broke through in 2008.

Virginia was "built to fail in March" right up until Tony Bennett guided the Cavaliers to a redemptive 2019 national title. So was Purdue until Matt Painter coached the Boilermakers to the 2024 championship game. Gonzaga, too, even as Mark Few reeled off nine consecutive runs to at least the NCAA tournament's second weekend, including title game appearances in 2017 and 2021.

The lesson is that the untrustworthy-in-March label isn't permanent. Elite teams don't always advance in a single-elimination tournament known for chaos and upsets, but the best coaches keep knocking on the door until they bust through.

That's not to suggest that there's nothing Scheyer can learn from Duke's recent stretch of March flameouts. Maybe there's more he can do to help his players get an easy basket when the game pressure intensifies or to prevent a bad stretch from becoming an avalanche.

Duke may not have a national player of the year frontrunner in its starting five this season like it did the past two years, but the Blue Devils make up for it with exceptional height and depth. Who else in college basketball could have a rotation with no players shorter than 6-foot-4? Or a second unit that features multiple five-star recruits and could easily be a Top 25-caliber starting five elsewhere?

Four of last year's six-leading scorers are back, a rare luxury for a program that has chosen to sacrifice roster continuity to chase one-and-done talent. Big man Patrick Ngongba has gradually expanded his offensive toolbox. Onetime 3-and-D specialist Dame Sarr has also developed into a more complete offensive threat.

Scheyer complemented that core group of returners by adding another highly rated freshman class led by 17-year-old Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje, a skilled 7-footer who earned MVP honors while leading the U.S. U-17 World Cup team to a gold medal this past summer. Boumtje Boumtje is not eligible for the NBA Draft until 2028 and is expected to develop for two seasons in Durham.

Perhaps unsure if there was a clear go-to scorer on the roster, Scheyer went out and added a player via the transfer portal who has experience in that role. Six-foot-5 shooting guard John Blackwell started every game for a 24-win Wisconsin team last season and averaged nearly 20 points.

Is this year's team capable of ending Duke's 12-year championship drought? Yes, especially if Scheyer can manage the egos of the five-star recruits who will be coming off the bench and turn the Blue Devils' depth into a weapon.

Will Duke's championship window close if this team falls short? No, not even close. With Boumtje Boumtje expected back and three more heralded recruits already signed for next year, the Blue Devils once again will be loaded.

That's why those who poke fun at Scheyer's NCAA tournament meltdowns should get in their jabs while they still can. Under Scheyer, Duke is operating at an even higher level than it was at the end of Krzyzewski's tenure.

As long as he doesn't get tempted by an offer to coach an NBA team, Scheyer is going to win that elusive national title sooner or later.

articles.title: Warriors Open To Draymond Green Trade Offers As Western Conference Rival Emerges As Potential Suitor
articles.summary: Draymond Green's 15th season with the Warriors could prove to be his last.
articles.body:
Draymond Green has been the heart and soul of the Golden State Warriors for over a decade, but his time with the team could come to an end before this season's trade deadline. The Athletic's NBA insider Sam Amick appeared on The TK Show , where he touched on Green's future with the Warriors.

"Of course they're going to listen to deals about Draymond at the deadline," Amick said. "And he knows that; we know that. You can say the quiet part out loud. You know, it did happen last year when the [Milwaukee] Bucks were certainly under the strong impression that if they were going to do something with the Warriors for Giannis [Antetokounmpo] that Draymond would be involved."

Now, Green cannot be traded until Dec. 15 as the Warriors signed him to a one-year, $27.7 million deal in the summer. The four-time All-Star only getting a one-year contract also indicated, though, that his future was uncertain.

Green has expressed a desire to retire with the Warriors , but he'd have to take a substantial pay cut for that. It's unclear if the 36-year-old would be willing to do that.

Green is averaging 2.8 points, 4.9 rebounds, 7.6 assists, 1.0 steals, and 0.9 blocks per game for the Warriors in 2026-27. Those aren't great numbers, and that is actually a career-low for points, but he remains an excellent defensive player.

Numbers also never really showed Green's true value to the Warriors anyway. He has been notably mocked for "triple-singles" over the years, but there's a reason the Warriors still kept him around.

Green might finally be on his way out this season, though, before the Feb. 11 trade deadline, and Amick thinks the Warriors would strongly consider a move if they can get anything for him. He later pointed to the Sacramento Kings as a potential suitor.

"He's a Michigan man, and Scott Perry, the Kings GM, has got deep Michigan ties and they have a very good relationship," Amick said. "I mean, Scott has known Draymond since he was literally a kid coming around the [Detroit] Pistons legendary teams in the Isiah Thomas days with Joe Dumars. So, there's some connective tissue there.

"And I might be overstating this, I have been so impressed with Draymond's kind of framing of his own situation in terms of what might lie ahead, where I could almost see him just embracing the lack of winning for the opportunity to [mentor]," Amick continued. "He literally has already pulled Darius Acuff aside… I could see that on a daily basis being really valuable to the Kings."

Green and Kings general manager Scott Perry are both Michigan natives, and Amick thinks that could play a factor. The forward also notably shared advice with rookie Darius Acuff Jr. , another Michigan native, when the Warriors faced them in preseason.

Winning has been Green's top priority for much of his career, and he has won four NBA championships with the Warriors. Amick thinks he might now be willing to accept that mentorship role on rebuilding teams, which so many veterans take on. Only time will tell if he is.

If this season does indeed prove to be the end of Green's time with the Warriors, he'll be walking away with his head held high. They had selected him with the No. 35 pick in the 2012 NBA Draft, and he became a pillar for one of the greatest dynasties in modern NBA history.

articles.title: 'Don't Matter,' AJ Dybantsa Reacts to Highlight Video From Wizards vs. Pistons, 'Need More Dubs'
articles.summary: Despite his own individual success early in his rookie season, AJ Dybantsa is only focused on helping the Washington Wizards win more games.
articles.body:
Despite his own individual success early in his rookie season, AJ Dybantsa is only focused on helping the Washington Wizards win more games.

After ESPN posted a highlight video on X of Dybantsa's performance in Monday's 122-111 loss to the Detroit Pistons, the Wizards forward quoted it by writing "don't matter. need more dubs."

Against a Pistons team that has the No. 3 defensive rating in the NBA, Dybantsa put up 21 points on 8-of-17 shooting with eight rebounds and two blocks in 37 minutes.

Despite the additions of Anthony Davis and Trae Young into the lineup, the Wizards are struggling offensively. They rank 23rd in rating and 26th in points per game.

Those issues have started to show up amid the Wizards' ongoing four-game losing streak after a 4-3 start. They have allowed at least 114 points in every game during this skid.

Washington's schedule has been difficult with two games against the Atlanta Hawks, followed by road games against the Oklahoma City Thunder and Pistons.

Things won't get much easier for a bit after Wednesday night against the Indiana Pacers. The Wizards' following three games will be at home vs. the Pistons, Houston Rockets and Memphis Grizzlies.

Washington's 4-7 record overall is tied with the Charlotte Hornets for ninth in the Eastern Conference. On the bright side, the Wizards' fourth win last season didn't come until Dec. 14, so this is positive progress.

Dybantsa, the No. 1 pick in the 2026 NBA draft, has started seven straight games after missing the first four games of the regular season due to a sprained ankle. He is averaging 16.7 points, 6.1 rebounds and 2.1 assists per contest.

articles.title: ‘Need to be talked about’ – Kyrie Irving addresses ‘social issues’ in the WNBA
articles.summary: The WNBA continues to attract the attention of some of the biggest NBA stars. It feels like the WNBA can never catch a break from being pulled into every cul...
articles.body:
The WNBA continues to attract the attention of some of the biggest NBA stars.

It feels like the WNBA can never catch a break from being pulled into every culture war online. Whether people are arguing over trans athletes or throwing around toxic accusations about social issues, the actual hoops always seem to get overshadowed by bad-faith debates.

Caitlin Clark found herself shoved right into the middle of that mess, with people using her name to push talking points. She eventually stepped up to clear the air, bluntly calling out the hate and making it crystal clear she wants no part of people using her to bring other women down.

Kyrie Irving gives his views on the WNBA

Kyrie Irving didn't hold back when talking about the WNBA. He gave the players tons of credit for sticking together and pushing the game forward, but he made sure to call out what still needs to change: seeing more Black women actually getting hired as head coaches on the sidelines.

"Yeah, I think there's definitely a big desire for more black female head coaches to be involved into the W. And you're just seeing the league grow tremendously. And I think a lot of the social issues that are talked about are very relevant and they need to be talked about.

"So I'm grateful you asked that question, but I think our W in general just does a great job of staying connected, staying united, doing things for each other, and advocating for the things that they want. So I'm really proud of our women, really proud of my sisters over there. But we definitely do need to see a lot more black head coaches over there."

Jemele Hill called it out first when guys kept getting tapped for WNBA coaching gigs , and Kyrie just put his finger on another real blind spot with the lack of Black female head coaches.

They aren't wrong either, as these are conversations to have. But damn if it isn't exhausting watching non-basketball topics steal all the oxygen the second the basketball itself is starting to take off.

articles.title: Jimmy Butler's Clipboard Message to Warriors Revealed by Steve Kerr After Blowout Win vs. Pelicans
articles.summary: Injured Golden State Warriors star Jimmy Butler had a simple idea for how to achieve success during his team's 138-87, blowout win over the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday night.
articles.body:
Injured Golden State Warriors star Jimmy Butler had a simple idea for how to achieve success during his team's 138-87, blowout win over the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday night.

Butler was seen on the sidelines holding a clipboard with some writing on it, and Warriors head coach Steve Kerr revealed the message, telling reporters that it read, "Pass to Steph," in reference to superstar guard Stephen Curry:

The 37-year-old Butler made a departure from his usual look by dressing up like the Warriors' coaches on Monday, which is an idea Kerr came up with before the game.

"It was funny because I don't know how this happened, but I told [assistant coach] Khalid [Robinson] about five minutes before the game, I told Khalid, 'One of these days, we should have Jimmy dress up like us' because he's always got some great outfit on and something fashionable, and we wear our quarter-zips and sweaters," Kerr said. "I said, 'We should really get him to dress like a coach one day,' and then he walks out, and he's dressed like us. I turned to Khalid, I said, 'Did you tell him to do that?' and he goes, 'No.' It was, I guess, mental telepathy or something. We're on the same page on that. He was enjoying himself."

Kerr was even impressed with the coaching job Butler did, saying, "He said all the right things, you know, team fouls, you know, how many team fouls we had, like he was really acting the part."

Curry finished with 25 points, which is fairly modest by his standards, but he did tie for the team lead in scoring on Monday with Brandin Podziemski.

Golden State mostly benefited from a balanced attack with three players scoring over 20 points and six scoring in double digits.

Since starting the season 0-3, the Dubs have been on a roll, reeling off eight consecutive victories.

Making that run of success even more impressive is the fact that Butler has yet to play as he continues to recover from a torn ACL that cut his 2025-26 season short.

Until Butler is able to return to the court, it appears as though he has found a new role that suits him quite well.

Butler's next chance to lend a helping hand to the Golden State coaching staff will come Wednesday when the Warriors go on the road to face the Houston Rockets.

articles.title: Victor Wembanyama Praised by Devin Booker After Spurs-Suns, 'Something Like We've Never Seen Before'

Phoenix Suns guard Devin Booker marveled Monday night at another eye-popping performance by San Antonio Spurs superstar center Victor Wembanyama.

Despite playing just 25 minutes, Wembanyama dropped 40 points on 15-of-19 shooting to go along with 11 rebounds, nine blocks and three assists.

Rising Stars Who Could Make Their 1st All-NBA Team ⭐

articles.title: Cooper Flagg Joins Kevin Durant, Makes NBA History With Rare Stat in Mavs' Win vs. Pacers
articles.summary: Second-year Dallas Mavericks star Cooper Flagg joined elite company with his performance against the Indiana Pacers on Monday night.
articles.body:
Second-year Dallas Mavericks star Cooper Flagg joined elite company with his performance against the Indiana Pacers on Monday night.

In Dallas' 125-122 win, Flagg became only the second teenager in NBA history to record at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a single game, per the NBA's official X account:

Rising Stars Who Could Make Their 1st All-NBA Team ⭐

The only other player to reach those milestones in the same game as a teenager was future Hall of Famer Kevin Durant, who dropped 42 points, 13 rebounds and six assists in the final game of his rookie season with the Seattle SuperSonics in 2007-08.

Flagg, who doesn't turn 20 until next month, has been every bit as good as advertised at the NBA level thus far.

Selected first overall in the 2025 NBA draft out of Duke, Flagg was named NBA Rookie of the Year last season by virtue of averaging 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists per game.

Flagg has leveled up his play thus far in his second season, averaging 25.9 points, 6.9 rebounds, 6.9 assists and 2.2 steals per contest.

On top of that, Flagg has the Mavs playing strong team basketball after missing the playoffs each of the previous two seasons and winning only 26 games during his rookie campaign.

Dallas currently sits ninth in the Western Conference with a 7-4 record, placing it firmly in playoff contention.

articles.title: College basketball’s rules are being rewritten in real time. Coaches are scrambling to keep up
articles.summary: College basketball is a hot mess, as it has been many times before. The difference now is that the bending – or breaking – of the rules comes via a court order.
articles.body: Mark Pope is not like most college basketball coaches. It has nothing to do with his Rhodes Scholar candidacy or the three years he spent at Columbia’s Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons, intent on becoming a doctor. No, the great separator between Pope and his peers is that he is an optimist. He sees sunshine while everyone else dodges raindrops. He embraces hope instead of giving in to despair. And this season, while everyone else is Eeyore-ing about, morosely shuffling to work as if they are being asked to dig ditches with a spoon, Pope leans back into a chair at a conference-room table inside his University of Kentucky basketball offices and says the single craziest thing anyone has said to date about college basketball in 2026. “It’s the best time to be a coach, man,” he says. “It’s gotta be, right?” The punch line does not come. He is dead serious. To be clear, college basketball is a hot mess. This is not an opinion. Months after Lane Kiffin threatened near-anarchy by attempting to use the court system to run an end-around the eligibility rules, college hoops is effectively saying, “Hold my beer.” There are currently 54 players competing in the SEC, Big Ten, Big East, ACC and Big 12 thanks to temporary restraining orders that granted them relief to play an additional fifth year. Another 15 others have not been cleared despite similar attempts. The court systems have made such a mockery of roster construction that Sports Illustrated went so far as to create a tracker showing who can and cannot play and how each case was decided. It does not, however, account for the international players who have been given the OK after competing in various overseas pro leagues and are, at best, well past the expired date for typical college-aged students. Nor does it account for the endless number of players who have changed school jerseys via the traditional transfer portal. “We are at the forefront of the chaotic instability,” Vanderbilt coach Mark Byington told CNN Sports before the season started. “We’re leading it.” The chaos has created an orange-dimpled Venn diagram. On one side sit the teams and coaches that have fully embraced the chaos (think LSU’s Will Wade) and on the other are those who have given it the stiff arm (hello, Michigan State’s Tom Izzo). In the gray lives the rest: those who are either morally opposed but competitively willing, or morally indifferent and competitively willing. “It’s a constantly changing landscape,” says Gonzaga’s Mark Few, who has added two fifth-year players and is waiting on a third. “One thing I’ve tried to focus on is how do you serve Gonzaga the best, and how do you put the best team on the floor and the best product out there and stick to our core values and protect our culture?” A long history in the gray area of morality College basketball has long lived in the gray. Those waxing nostalgic for the good old days might want to check their rose-colored lenses. The phonebook thickness of what once was the NCAA rulebook was largely written by college basketball coaches who cleverly found ways to exploit loopholes, when they weren’t skirting them altogether. This is the sport in which an envelope stuffed with cash put Kentucky on probation and a fixer hanging with players in a hot tub did the same at UNLV. As toothless as the FBI investigation into college hoops wound up being, people still went to jail for paying players under the table and long before he made end-around offers, Will Wade made “strong ass” ones on a wiretap. “I have a few older guys on my staff – Rick Ray, Rodney Terry – and I’ll say to them, ‘This is the craziest time in college basketball,” Byington says. “They just look at me and laugh and say, ‘It’s not even close.” The difference is now the bending – or breaking – of the rules via a court order. The NCAA’s decision to pivot to a five-in-five model (essentially allowing college athletes five years of eligibility) was widely lauded. It ends the endless waiver requests that had besieged sports, and puts a cap, if you will, on how long a person can stay in college. But the national office adopted the rule in June, slightly messy for college football but an abject disaster for hoops. The new legislation arrived on the same day of the NBA Draft, too late for would-be fifth years to reconsider their decisions to go pro, and just early enough that those who did go through the process hadn’t fully signed contracts or made deals to head overseas. That purgatory left such enough wiggle room to argue the timing was entirely unfair. And so came the lawsuits, waves of them, with players seeking an extension of their college careers – not because they missed campus but because, for many, NIL deals would be far more lucrative than whatever a pseudo-professional deal might look like. Suddenly coaches accustomed to studying ball-screens, became paralegals. Pope can recite chapter and verse on the differences between the TRO rulings in the case brought in California versus Ohio. Florida coach Todd Golden, whose father is an attorney, willingly went deep into the weeds to understand the various cases. “I believe it’s my job as a leader of this program to know what we’re up against, what we’re arguing and fighting for,” Golden said at SEC media day. “I’ve taken a pretty big legal interest in what we’re going through here in college sports.” The head-spinning world of building a roster While the courts were ruling on fifth-year players, the NCAA was working through complicated international players, and the portal was sifting its usual numbers through its window (2,500 or so entered). Taken together, it all made roster construction, once the very backbone of building a successful program, feel more like a blindfolded dart contest. Teams aren’t being built so much as assembled; they’re more like Lincoln logs prone to quick crumbling than Legos snapped into place with some semblance of stability. “You’re always making educated guesses on the team you’re putting together,” Pope said. “It’s just now you’re making an educated guess on the court system. You’re trying to dig into where the case is going, looking for trends and trying to understand how your league is going to respond. It’s not just educated guesses on what players you want to take into your program; it’s on the rules.” It is, however, head-spinning. Duke Brennan played at Grand Canyon two seasons ago, Villanova last year and now is at Oklahoma. Xaivian Lee spent three seasons at Princeton, last year at Florida and is now at Gonzaga. Traveling: It’s not just a whistle anymore. Will Wade had four players on his roster as recently as September; now he has 14. Trey Kaufman-Renn announced he’d transfer from Purdue to Kansas in mid-October as he sought a sixth year of eligibility. He didn’t play in the Jayhawks’ exhibition game but entered in the second half in the season opener against Fordham. Just last week – and a day before its second game of the season – Saint Louis learned that Robbie Avila, the goggle-wearing “Cream Abdul Jabaar,” was cleared to play. And then before he could suit up for his first game, the College Sports Commission said Avila was out. Where once the NCAA limited scholarships, now it sets roster spots. The Billikens had a full roster, and the CSC ruled they could not add Avila to the list. And then there is the most amusing twist of all. In August, Mark Mitchell, who had played at Missouri, committed to Kentucky after receiving a TRO. But the SEC ruled that Mitchell couldn’t transfer because he didn’t enter the portal during the typical window (he was, at the time, making a go at the NBA Draft). Mitchell returned to Mizzou but the Kentucky Court of Appeals dissolved his TRO. In October, a Kentucky judge reversed the reversal. He’s eligible to play for the Tigers and, in fact, will face Kentucky in January. “That’s the risk when you go all in,” Pope says philosophically. “That’s the fascinating part, really. There are so many dynamics at work and it changes every day.” Instant experience Equally interesting: Who is taking the risks is who isn’t. Among those ranked in the preseason top 10, six schools (Duke, Illinois, UConn, Michigan State, Texas and Virginia) didn’t even try to add players via the courts, three others (Arizona, Tennessee and Houston) tried and failed to add just one extra fifth-year and Florida brought in just Denzel Aberdeen. The numbers may explain why some of the best teams aren’t going all in. About a decade ago, Ken Pomeroy added continuity to his famed stats. It’s a complex matrix but essentially boils down to how much a roster has played together. Of the six schools opting out of fifth-year players altogether, all but Texas rank in the top 100 in continuity. Not only were older players adding significantly more value, but their variability was also considerably less. As a group, veteran players were consistently more valuable than talented freshmen. And that’s the real driving force behind all of this. Throughout whatever iteration has come its way, college basketball’s one constant is that experience wins. Only one national champion in the last decade – UConn in 2023 – has failed to rank in the top 100 in either continuity or Division I experience per KenPom. But getting old takes time and plenty of coaches aren’t so sure they have it. Look at that list again. The common thread: Job security. Izzo, Golden and Dan Hurley each have won a national title and Jon Scheyer and Brad Underwood have taken Duke and Illinois respectively to a Final Four. Ryan Odom is only in his second year at Virginia, but the Cavaliers exist by being an outlier to the usual way of doing business in college basketball. So many others – not all but many – feeling the squeeze of instant satisfaction from itchy fan bases and twitchy administrations, or the march of their own internal professional clocks, are opting to fast-track experience. Fifth-year players, thereby, became very attractive in this loophole season for the same reason that portal players have been appealing for years now. They are microwavable versions of experience. The only real question, of course, is will it work? Come April in Detroit, will a championship-winning coach have to thank his local circuit judge along with his administration? Will a court order find its way into Springfield? “I am so fascinated to see how this all shakes out,” Pope says. “I mean, really? How much fun is this?” He was being rhetorical, but he was also being serious.
